blocks.text: How much damage swarms of locusts inflict on the regions of Syria and Egypt will be better understood from what the writers of histories as well as of travels report to us. GREGORIUS BARHEBRAEUS, also called ABULPHARAGIUS, in his Chronicle, written in Syriac, copied by Bruns from the Bodleian codex and edited by Kirsch, p. 134: ܒܫܢܬ ܐܨܗ ܕܝ̈ܘܢܝܐ ܐܬܐ ܩܡܨܐ ܦܪܚܐ ܘܚܒܠ ܙܪ̈ܥܐ ܘܐܪܡܝ ܙܪܥܐ ܘܢܦܩ. ܘܡܫܬܟܚ ܗܘܐ ܘܣܠܩ ܒܫܘܪ̈ܐ ܘܐܣ̈ܐ. ܘܥܐܠ ܡܢ ܟܘ̈ܐ ܘܬܪ̈ܥܐ ܠܒ̈ܬܐ. ܘܐܬܡܠܝܘ ܡܢܗ ܐܦ ܓܪ̈ܒܐ ܕܡ̈ܝܐ ܘܬܫܘܝ̈ܬܐ ܘܦܬܘܪ̈ܐ ܘܠܓ̈ܢܐ. ܘܟܕ ܡܢ ܦܢܝܬ ܬܝܡܢܐ ܥܐܠ ܗܘܐ ܠܒܝܬܐ ܡܢ ܓܒܐ ܓܪܒܝܝܐ ܢܦܩ ܗܘܐ. ܘܐܟܠ ܥܡ ܥܣܒܐ ܘܐܝܠ̈ܢܐ. ܐܦ ܡܐ̈ܢܐ ܕܥܡܪܐ ܘܢܚ̈ܬܐ ܕܒ̈ܢܝܢܫܐ. ܘܟܕ ܓܡܪ ܠܟܠܗ ܦܢܝܬܐ ܕܐܘܪܗܝ ܘܣܪܘܓ ܥܒܪ ܠܡܥܪܒܐ. In the year of the Greeks 1095 (which was 784 after Christ) flying locusts swarmed in, ruined the crops, and laid eggs; and those hatched from them, once they had grown wings, climbed the walls and partitions and entered the houses through the windows and doors [Cf. Exod. X, 6. ומלאו בתיך ובתי כל עבדיך ובתי כל מצרים, They shall fill, the locusts, your houses, and those of your courtiers and subjects]. The water jars, floors, tables and dishes were filled with them. After entering the houses on the south side, they went out on the north side, having consumed the plants, the trees, even the woollen garments and clothing of men. Having laid waste the whole region of Edessa and Sarug, they passed on towards the west. And the continuator of Barhebraeus, in dem Neuen Repertorio für bibl. und morgenl. Literat. edited by Paulus, vol. 1, p. 67 f. [the Syriac, 10 lines, not transcribed here]: In the year 1774 (1463 after Christ) many locusts came from the east, and indeed wingless ones [So, it seems, the words ܘܕܒܒܐ ܐܝܬܝܗܘܢ ܗܘܐ should be rendered, which Bruns translated: and flies swarmed in. But ܕܒܒܐ here undoubtedly agrees in meaning with the Arabic دُبَّاءٌ [dubbāʾ], a locust not yet winged]. They came as far as Egypt, ate the crops, vineyards, fruits, trees, even the grass, and left nothing green on the face of the earth. The vineyards, fruits and trees failed, stripped and devoured by the locusts. LEO AFRICANUS in the Descript. Africae [III, 284] book 2, Chapter 11, p. 77, Zurich edition of 1559: While I was staying among them (the people of Tagtessa), a great multitude of locusts had invaded that region, which I would venture to affirm had grown so large that they far exceeded the ears of grain, which at that time had reached maturity; so much so that the very surface of the ground was entirely covered with locusts. [Cf. Exod. X, 15. ויכס את עין כל הארץ ותחשך הארץ They covered the whole surface of the earth and darkened it]. And this in the year 919, which was 1510 of Christ. The same Leo, book 9, ch. 61, p. 512: Locusts are generally seen in Africa in such numbers that in flight, like a cloud, they cover the rays of the sun. They devour the trees themselves together with their leaves and fruit. When about to depart they leave eggs, from which others (though they do not fly) spring forth; and wherever they are encountered they eat everything down to the bark of the trees, and leave behind a great dearth of grain, especially in Mauritania. LE BRUN, Voyages au Levant p. 252, mentions a swarm of locusts which within the space of two hours had consumed everything green, and the places in Cyprus through which these insects had passed were as if laid waste by fire. Russell reports the same, Natural History of Aleppo p. 62 (Of the noxious kind may well be reckoned the locust, which sometimes arrive in such incredible multitudes, that it would appear fabulous to relate, destroying the whole of the verdure where-ever they pass). Whoever wants more should consult OEDMANN in den Vermischten Sammlungen fasc. 2, Chapter 6, p. 95 ff., and our Scholia on Exod. X, 14. p. 450 ff., second edition.
In Egypt barley ripens in the month of February; wheat lasts until the end of March, says Forsskål in the Prolegomenn. ad Flor. Aegypt. p. XLIII.
Compare the passage of Barhebraeus cited above, note 1.
